introduction: Macbeth returns from defending Scotland to hear a prophecy that seems to offer him a future beyond military honor. When one part quickly proves true, the possibility of kingship begins to reshape his loyalty, his marriage, and his understanding of choice. Lady Macbeth urges him toward the opportunity she sees in the prediction, while Banquo warns that truthful promises may serve destructive purposes. The struggle turns on what Macbeth decides to do with words whose apparent certainty conceals dangerous limits.

fullSynopsis.text: Three witches prepare to meet Macbeth after a battle in which he and Banquo have defended Duncan's kingdom. They hail Macbeth as Thane of Glamis, Thane of Cawdor, and future king, while promising that Banquo will father kings without becoming one himself. Duncan has already awarded Macbeth the traitor Cawdor's title, and its confirmation makes the larger prophecy seem credible. Banquo warns against trusting powers that offer small truths to lead men into harm. Macbeth's thoughts nevertheless turn toward murder, particularly when Duncan names Malcolm his heir.

Lady Macbeth reads her husband's account and resolves to overcome the scruples that might keep him from the crown. Duncan's visit to their castle creates an opportunity. Macbeth recognizes the duties of kinship, allegiance, and hospitality that forbid murdering him, and initially withdraws from the plan. Lady Macbeth attacks his courage and proposes drugging Duncan's guards and blaming them. Macbeth agrees. On his way to the chamber, he sees a dagger that he recognizes may be a creation of his troubled mind. After killing Duncan, he returns horrified, carrying the daggers that should have remained with the guards. Lady Macbeth takes them back and smears the sleepers with blood.

Macduff discovers the king's body. Macbeth admits that he has killed the guards, presenting his act as furious loyalty rather than allowing them to answer. Malcolm and Donalbain flee to England and Ireland for safety, and their flight becomes grounds for suspicion. Macbeth is chosen king. Banquo suspects him but also considers the promise for his own descendants. Fearing Banquo and a succession that excludes his own line, Macbeth hires men to kill both him and Fleance. Banquo dies in the ambush, but Fleance escapes. At the royal banquet, Macbeth sees Banquo's ghost and speaks so wildly that Lady Macbeth dismisses the guests.

Macbeth resolves to consult the witches again. Hecate prepares deceptive apparitions to draw him into ruin through confidence, while Scottish nobles increasingly look toward Malcolm and Macduff in England. The apparitions warn him about Macduff but assure him that no one born of a woman can harm him and that he will not be defeated until Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane. He interprets these limits as practical guarantees of safety. A vision of a procession of kings descended from Banquo troubles him nonetheless. Learning that Macduff has fled, Macbeth orders the slaughter of his household. His murderers kill Macduff's son and pursue Lady Macduff; Ross later reports that wife, children, and servants were killed.

In England Malcolm tests Macduff by falsely claiming monstrous vices. Macduff's despair for Scotland convinces him of the thane's loyalty, and Malcolm reveals that he has English military support. The news of his family's murder turns Macduff's grief toward a personal reckoning with Macbeth. At Dunsinane a doctor observes Lady Macbeth sleepwalking, reliving the crimes and trying to wash imaginary blood from her hands. Macbeth clings to the prophecies while allies desert him. Malcolm orders his approaching soldiers to conceal their numbers behind cut branches from Birnam Wood. Lady Macbeth's death is announced, and Macbeth responds with a bleak meditation on life's emptiness before news of the moving wood shakes his confidence.

Macbeth fights on and kills young Siward. Confronted by Macduff, he still claims protection from any man born of a woman, until Macduff reveals that he was cut from his mother's womb before his time. Recognizing the promises' double meanings, Macbeth nevertheless refuses capture and resumes combat. Macduff returns with his head and hails Malcolm as king. Malcolm rewards his supporters as earls, plans the return of exiles and punishment of the tyrant's agents, and invites them to his coronation at Scone. He describes Lady Macbeth's death as a suspected suicide.

acts.label: ACT I
acts.summary: The witches plan their encounter with Macbeth while Duncan hears of his valor against rebellion and Norway. The king grants him the condemned Cawdor's title. On the heath, Macbeth and Banquo hear predictions of Macbeth's kingship and Banquo's royal descendants; confirmation of the new title encourages Macbeth's interest despite Banquo's warning. Duncan's designation of Malcolm as heir makes Macbeth see an obstacle to his desires. At Inverness, Lady Macbeth reads his letter and resolves to drive him toward the crown. She welcomes Duncan with outward devotion while preparing his death. Macbeth considers the moral claims against murdering his king and guest, but her challenge to his courage and plan to frame the guards bring him back to the conspiracy.

acts.label: ACT II
acts.summary: Banquo admits dreaming of the witches, while Macbeth conceals his concern. Alone, Macbeth sees an unreal dagger directing him toward Duncan and follows Lady Macbeth's signal. He returns after the murder shaken by blood, prayer, and the imagined destruction of sleep. Refusing to revisit the chamber, he leaves Lady Macbeth to return the daggers and incriminate the drugged guards. A drunken porter delays admitting Macduff and Lennox, joking that he keeps hell's gate. Macduff finds Duncan dead; Macbeth kills the guards and explains the act as uncontrollable grief. Fearing further danger, Malcolm and Donalbain separate into exile. Their flight attracts suspicion, while reports of unnatural events accompany news that Macbeth has been chosen king and gone to Scone.

acts.label: ACT III
acts.summary: Banquo suspects Macbeth's means of becoming king but remembers the promise to his own descendants. Macbeth, troubled by that rival future, engages murderers to kill Banquo and Fleance while concealing the plan from his wife. Banquo is killed, but his son escapes. At the banquet Macbeth receives that incomplete report and then sees Banquo's ghost occupying his place. His terrified responses unsettle the guests; Lady Macbeth attempts to explain them as a familiar illness before ending the gathering. Macbeth turns toward further violence and another consultation with the witches. Hecate reproaches them for acting without her and plans illusions that will encourage destructive certainty. Lennox and another lord discuss the suffering kingdom and the hope of resistance supported from England.

acts.label: ACT IV
acts.summary: The witches' ritual produces apparitions warning Macbeth against Macduff while promising protection from anyone born of a woman and defeat only when Birnam Wood reaches Dunsinane. Macbeth trusts the apparent impossibility of these conditions, though the vision of Banquo's royal descendants disturbs him. Hearing Macduff has fled, he orders the destruction of his family and household. Lady Macduff questions her husband's departure before murderers arrive, kill her son, and pursue her. In England Malcolm pretends to have overwhelming vices to test Macduff's motives, then retracts the claims when Macduff despairs for Scotland. They prepare to return with Siward and English troops. Ross reports the household's slaughter, and Macduff insists on feeling his grief as well as seeking revenge.

acts.label: ACT V
acts.summary: Lady Macbeth sleepwalks before witnesses, repeating fragments of the crimes and trying to cleanse imagined blood. Macbeth arms himself despite desertion and relies on the prophetic assurances. Malcolm's army carries Birnam branches to conceal its strength. After learning his wife is dead, Macbeth reflects on life's futility; a report that the wood is moving forces him to confront deceptive meanings. He fights and kills young Siward, but Macduff reveals that he was cut from his mother's womb before his time, destroying Macbeth's remaining assurance. Macbeth refuses surrender and dies fighting. Macduff displays his head and proclaims Malcolm king. Malcolm makes his thanes earls, proposes restoration and justice, reports suspected suicide in Lady Macbeth's case, and summons his supporters to a coronation at Scone.
